slides.say: Given: four times the absolute value of x, plus twelve times the absolute value of y, is forty-four. And x plus three times the absolute value of y is one. What is x?

Two equations, two unknowns, and absolute values. It looks scary, but it's really not. [short pause] We'll solve it three ways. The full algebra, a shorter algebra that ends with the answers, and plugging in the answers right away.

[short pause] Our first method, the algebra. Four, twelve and forty-four can all be divided by four. Four over four is one, twelve over four is three, and forty-four over four is eleven. So the first equation becomes the absolute value of x, plus three times the absolute value of y, is eleven.
at: can all be divided by four

slides.say: They ask for x, so I want to get rid of y. How do I do that? I subtract the second equation from the first. Three times the absolute value of y cancels, and eleven minus one is ten. So the absolute value of x, minus x, is ten.

With absolute values, I want the bars alone on one side and everything else on the other. Why? Because then I can open the bars into two options, just like bars equal to a number. So I add x to both sides, and the absolute value of x is ten plus x.
at: the absolute value of x is ten plus x

slides.say: Now two options, the sides are equal, or one is the opposite of the other. Option one, x is ten plus x. Take x off both sides, x minus x is zero, so zero is ten. That's false, so no solution here.
Option two, x is minus ten minus x. Add x to both sides, x plus x is two x, so two x is minus ten. Minus ten divided by two is minus five, so x is minus five.
A letter on the right side, so let's check. Ten plus minus five is five, and the absolute value of minus five is five. It works. Minus five, choice number two is our answer.
[pause] Our second method. The same algebra, until we get to the absolute value of x is ten plus x. And then, instead of solving it, I plug in the answers. They're all numbers.
Minus two. Its absolute value is two, and ten plus minus two is eight. Two isn't eight, out. Minus five. Its absolute value is five, and ten plus minus five is five. Yes.

And choice numbers three and four, three and five? For a positive x the bars do nothing, so the absolute value of x is just x. Then x is ten plus x, and that's impossible. So choice numbers three and four are out too.

[pause] Our third method, plugging in the answers from the very start. Choice number one, x is minus two. Into the second equation, minus two plus three times the absolute value of y is one. Add two to both sides, one plus two is three, so three times the absolute value of y is three. Three divided by three is one, so the absolute value of y is one.
Now the first equation. Four times two is eight, twelve times one is twelve, and eight plus twelve is twenty. Not forty-four, out.

Choice number two, x is minus five. Minus five plus three times the absolute value of y is one. Add five to both sides, one plus five is six, so three times the absolute value of y is six. Six divided by three is two, so the absolute value of y is two.
First equation. Four times five is twenty, twelve times two is twenty-four, and twenty plus twenty-four is forty-four. It works.

In the exam you'd circle it and move on. Here, let's quickly see three and five. x is three. Three plus three times the absolute value of y is one, so take three off, one minus three is negative two. But an absolute value can't be negative, so it's out. x is five, one minus five is negative four, negative again. Out.
